newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya deal involves trouble at every turn.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya deal involves trouble at every turn.

text.p: The peace deal signed by Russian security chief Alexander Lebed and Chechen rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov on August 31 has come closer than ever to ending the conflict in the separatist North Caucasus region.

It is the third such deal and the only one to address some of the political issues behind the fighting, which began when President Boris Yeltsin sent troops to Chechnya in December 1994 to end its three-year drive for secession.
But there are sticking points at every turn:

-- Withdrawal of Russian troops. Unlike previous peace deals, there is no provision in this agreement for rebel disarmament in return. This has upset the military, which feels its 21-month-old military campaign has been in vain, and raised fears that the rebels will just take over as soon as they leave. The pullout began on September 8 but stopped the next day.

-- Exchange of prisoners of war. Both sides dispute the lists of prisoners provided by the other. The Russians say some of those on the rebel list are not fighters but criminals. The rebels retort that the Russians are treating political prisoners as criminals in order to avoid handing them over. The military said it halted the pullout over this issue.

-- Establishment of an interim coalition government to pave the way for elections. The rebels have convened a congress of political organisations to work on this but Doku Zavgayev, the Moscow-backed Chechen leader who is still nominally in his job, has boycotted it. He says the troop withdrawal will lead to civil war. Russia is also concerned by the one-sidedness of the congress and a senior official said on Sunday that Moscow would not recognise the draft government list it had drawn up.

-- Deferral of discussion of Chechnya's status for five years. Both sides have taken advantage of this vague compromise to insist loudly on their former positions. The rebels have reaffirmed their commitment to their 1991 declaration of independence and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has warned them Moscow will never allow the region to split off.

-- Reconstruction of Chechnya. Moscow has said it will provide funds to repair the devastation in the region only to a commission made up of federal, rebel and pro-Moscow Chechen representatives, which so far does not exist. Even if it is set up, the distribution of funds is in doubt because Moscow can ill afford to pay and a large proportion of previous reconstruction funds was embezzled.
The only part of the deal which has worked so far is a ceasefire, which officially began on August 21.
There has been the occasional exchange of fire as well as allegations, which the rebels deny, that the separatists have murdered pro-Moscow officials.
But there has been none of the all-out fighting which killed tens of thousands since December 1994 and which flared seriously in Grozny on August 6, when the rebels seized much of the city.

The essence of problems with the latest deal seems, ironically, to be the very reason it provided hope in the first place: Lebed, hoping to build his own political career on the deal, conceded more than ever before to the rebels.
